steps.en: What you see: The anterior mitral leaflet moves toward the septum in systole and touches it in obstructive disease. M mode shows the classic systolic anterior motion spike with septal contact. The mitral jet points posteriorly in late systole, the reverse of prolapse. The resting gradient is 30 mmHg or more and rises with Valsalva, standing or exercise while squatting and leg raise ease it.

Normal values with units: Resting outflow gradient. Below 30 mmHg at rest is latent or non obstructive. Resting 30 to 49 mmHg is obstructive. Resting or provoked 50 mmHg or more is the threshold used when considering septal reduction.. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination guideline, section on Doppler and haemodynamics

Provoked gradient. Provoked 30 mmHg or more on Valsalva, standing or exercise confirms obstruction when rest is below 30 mmHg.. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination guideline, section on Doppler and haemodynamics

Septal thickness with narrow outflow. Asymmetric septal thickening of 15 mm or more with a narrow outflow tract underlies most obstruction.. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination guideline, section on left ventricular wall thickness

Mitral regurgitation direction. A posteriorly directed late systolic jet supports systolic anterior motion as the mechanism over primary leaflet disease.. Source: ASE 2017 valvular regurgitation guideline, section on mitral regurgitation quantitation

ECG and heart sound correlation ecg: Left ventricular hypertrophy with strain in lateral leads is typical. Deep septal Q waves with left axis appear in some patients. Atrial fibrillation in advanced disease worsens obstruction by losing atrial kick.

ECG and heart sound correlation sounds: A harsh late peaking systolic murmur grows louder with Valsalva and standing and eases with squatting or passive leg raise. This dynamic pattern is the reverse of most valve murmurs. A fourth sound marks the stiff ventricle.

What to report: Resting gradient with the exact provocation method and phase for each value
Septal contact timing on M mode with outflow width and septal thickness
Mitral jet direction and grade with anterior leaflet length and papillary position
Symptoms with triggers, drugs, volume status and family history for the septal reduction discussion
Red flags needing urgent referral: Syncope on exertion with a high provoked gradient, needs urgent inherited cardiac conditions review
Severe drug refractory symptoms with gradient 50 mmHg or more, needs urgent septal reduction assessment
Atrial fibrillation with rapid conduction in obstructive disease, needs urgent rhythm control on referral
Pitfalls: Nitrates, diuretics and ACE inhibitors worsen obstruction, so reconcile drugs before and after the study.
After alcohol septal ablation the gradient falls but scar arrhythmia risk persists, so follow up stays lifelong.
Mid cavity obstruction without septal contact needs a separate apical sweep, since contact is not the whole disease.

todo.en: How to get it on the probe, step by step: Start in the parasternal long axis and watch the anterior leaflet through systole for septal approach.
Record M mode through leaflet and septum to document contact and its timing.
Move to the apical three chamber view and align continuous wave Doppler through the outflow.
Record resting gradient, then repeat during Valsalva strain and immediately on standing.
Map the mitral jet direction and grade any posteriorly directed regurgitation.

Common mistakes and how to correct them: Contaminating the outflow signal with the mitral regurgitation jet. Fix: Sample from the apex with the beam through the outflow, not the mitral valve, and confirm the envelope peaks late.
Recording Valsalva too early or too late and missing the gradient rise. Fix: Give clear strain instructions and record during phase two of the manoeuvre when preload falls most.
Calling fixed obstruction when dehydration drives a dynamic gradient. Fix: Check volume status and vasodilators before labelling, since dehydration and nitrates exaggerate obstruction.

remember.en: Use the dynamic murmur and drug record to plan referral for septal reduction.

q.en: What defines systolic anterior motion on M mode?

o.en: Anterior motion toward the septum with contact in systole
Posterior motion away from the septum
No motion with a fixed orifice

why.en: The anterior leaflet moves toward the septum in systole and contact marks obstructive physiology.

q.en: How does the obstructive murmur behave with Valsalva?

o.en: It eases with Valsalva and standing
It grows louder with Valsalva and standing

why.en: Falling preload narrows the outflow further, so the murmur grows louder, the reverse of aortic stenosis.

q.en: Which resting gradient band means obstructive disease?

why.en: Resting 30 to 49 mmHg is obstructive, and 50 mmHg or more enters the septal reduction discussion.

q.en: Which jet direction supports systolic anterior motion over prolapse?

why.en: The displaced leaflet directs the jet posteriorly in late systole, opposite to anterior prolapse.

q.en: Exertional syncope occurs with a provoked gradient of 80 mmHg. What next?

o.en: Urgent inherited cardiac conditions review avoiding preload reducing drugs

why.en: High gradient syncope needs urgent specialist review, and nitrates and diuretics must be reviewed because they worsen obstruction.
